endorsements.title: Texas SB 1188 (89th Legislature), electronic health records and AI disclosure
endorsements.quote: any algorithm or decision assistance tool included in an electronic health record to assist a health care practitioner in making medical treatment decisions includes an individual's biological sex as recorded in the space described by Subdivision (1)(A).

commentary.bottom_line: No supplied study tests whether drawing biological sex from the statutorily designated EHR field changes the accuracy of treatment recommendations, and no supplied study documents the hazard. The practice rests on a single Texas statute that requires it.

perspectives.view: The evidence base for R501 contains zero studies testing the practice and zero studies documenting the hazard. Under GRADE conventions, certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. Any claim that the requirement reduces distorted recommendations remains untested in the material supplied.

Texas SB 1188 uses mandatory language. It requires that any algorithm or decision assistance tool in an EHR that assists treatment decisions include biological sex as recorded in the field the statute designates. For systems operating in Texas, compliance is a legal obligation regardless of the evidence gap.

No supplied study measures how often incorrect sex inputs reach decision algorithms or what harm follows. Without hazard data, the panel cannot estimate the frequency or severity of the failure this requirement targets. The panel also cannot say whether one designated field catches or introduces errors.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that compare treatment recommendations generated from the designated biological sex field against those generated from other sex or gender fields. These studies should measure how often recommendations differ, whether they lead to clinical errors, and how records for patients whose sex-linked physiology differs from the recorded value are handled.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The effect of the requirement on the accuracy of recommendations for these groups is unknown.
